source.title: Safety Offset Learning: When Benign Fine-Tuning Misaligns LLMs
source.authors: Jesson Wang; Zhanhao Hu; Minghao Lin; Yuchen Wu; Aylin Caliskan; Mengyuan Li

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether benign fine-tuning can increase harmful compliance, using a new construction based on rewritten benign instructions and refusal discrepancy, and reports held-out safety outcomes. It also tests conditions for transfer, but does not use the original study’s specific fine-tuning recipe.
record.gate_note: The paper measures harmful-prompt ASR and judge-rated harmfulness after fine-tuning, so its main results bear on V2; its explicit harmful-supervision reference bears on V1. The keyword experiment measures transfer from benign fine-tuning, not compliant-prefill, suffix, or decoding attacks. The paper does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, safety localization in parameters, or whether safety can be deepened. The in-distribution refusal diagnostics and refusal-log-probability comparisons concern training-input behavior or construction signals, not harmful-prompt compliance, and are not separate rows. The attempted refusal-target controls are described by the authors as non-discriminating because the models collapse into indiscriminate refusal.
record.test_reason: The study measures harmful-prompt ASR and judge HARM SCORE on three held-out benchmarks after fine-tuning three aligned models on benign data: ordinary Alpaca, prior selected benign sets, keyword-modified prompts, and SafeOff rewrites. This is a different construction aimed at V2. It also restates V2 as conditional: transfer needs a large refusal discrepancy with no surface shortcut. The LLM-LAT harmful-supervision reference bears on V1, though at 1000 examples. V3–V7 are not measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude benign fine-tuning degrades safety when it trains a large refusal-to-compliance transition that no surface shortcut can resolve. SafeOff does this across three models and three benchmarks without harmful content. They also explicitly report that degradation from ordinary or previously studied benign data is comparatively modest in their setting.
record.recipe_differences: Uses model-guided rewrites of benign instructions that elicit refusal, paired with the original harmless answers; tests behavioral-transition conditions rather than the original study’s harmful/benign fine-tuning recipe or few-example sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with keyword placement and count, SafeOff fraction, benchmark, model, and training-data construction. Fixed-position keywords transfer little despite high refusal discrepancy; scattered keywords transfer more as count grows. SafeOff effects strengthen at high data fractions. Table 1 uses one seed per cell.

fits_no_version.finding: Within selected v_proj coordinates, SafeOff LoRA updates have higher cosine similarity to harmful-fine-tuning updates than BASE does (0.13 vs 0.04 for LLM-LAT; 0.23 vs 0.20 for ShadowAlign).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-degrading benign fine-tuning shares an update direction with harmful fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: SafeOff rewrites raise the pre-fine-tuning log-probability of a fixed refusal string, including the first token, in 99.7% of 658 non-refused prompts (Table 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input rewrites shift refusal-sequence likelihood even without generated refusal; this is a construction diagnostic, not aligned-vs-base KL.

record.problems: The keyword-position grid uses one seed per cell. No error bars, confidence intervals, or other uncertainty estimates are reported for the tabulated results. ASR uses a substring refusal detector and HARM SCORE uses an LLM judge. The authors state that their attempted refusal-target controls are not discriminating because the models become indiscriminate refusers; they also note that held-out utility evaluation is limited.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the 12 utility-data mixture results in Table 10 (SAMSUM and GSM8K mixtures), the alternative-construction results in Table 7, the step-300 training-input refusal diagnostic in Table 3, the refusal-log-probability diagnostic in Table 8, and the attempted refusal-target controls in Table 9. The 60-row cap was prioritized for the main cross-model/benchmark comparison, the keyword transfer grid, and SafeOff ratio results. The authors themselves say the Table 9 safety-only outcome is not discriminating because both refusal-target models refuse benign held-out inputs indiscriminately.

untested.parts: The few-to-a-few-hundred example range. LLM-LAT is used only at the standard 1000-example LoRA setting, with no example-count sweep.
Full-parameter fine-tuning and closed or API models. Only LoRA (rank 8, q/v_proj) on 3–8B open models is used.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No prefilling, adversarial suffix or decoding attacks.
No test of safety localization in a small set of weights or ranks. The update-cosine diagnostic is not a localization test.
No test of whether data or objective makes safety token-shallow.

missing.what: Matched refusal-loss datasets L1–L4: same 100 sources and answers, rewrites at decreasing refusal loss. ADVBench HARM SCORE is 1.07, 1.62, 1.72, 2.03, against 1.00 for original data and 1.01 for the aligned model (Llama-3.1-8B, 250 steps, one seed).
Pre-fine-tuning baselines for Llama-3.1-8B on ADVBench: ASR 0.01, HARM SCORE 1.01. These are needed as baselines for the T1 and T4 rows.

Training trajectories: suffix-keyword runs show early harmful compliance then substantial recovery, while SafeOff stays elevated through step 1000 (Llama-3.2-3B). This bears on the persistence of benign-induced degradation.

record.verdict_notes: Table 4 gives no pre-fine-tuning column; comparisons were made against BASE. Aligned values (ASR 0.01, HS 1.01 for Llama-3.1-8B ADVBench) come from Table 9 and Sec 4.4. For Llama-3.2-3B at step 1000, Table 7 BASE (0.04/1.04) serves as reference. All runs use LoRA rank 8. Keyword grid and L1–L4 use one seed, and no uncertainty is reported. SafeOff is deliberately constructed per target model via refusal-likelihood beam search; it falls under V2's 'carefully chosen benign data' because targets are unchanged benign answers. A conditional restatement of V2 (T5-like) is also present. The reader's V1 limits_scope label was removed: the untested example range belongs under untested, not limits_scope.

versions.untested_parts: The harmful-supervision reference is evaluated, but the paper does not test fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred examples; the described standard setting uses 1000 examples.

The paper tests rewritten benign data, selected benign datasets, keyword-modified benign data, and mixtures/ratios. It does not establish that arbitrary ordinary benign instruction data raises harmful compliance.
No per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models is reported.
No compliant response prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change bypass is tested.
The update-cosine diagnostic does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
The paper tests behavioral discrepancy and shortcut conditions for transfer, not why safety is localized in early response tokens or whether data/objective causes that token-depth pattern.
No training intended to spread safety beyond the first response tokens, or evaluation of such deepening, is reported.
